title: Senior AD Engineer: Diagnosing a Silent Replication Drift
summary: Scenario question probing systematic replication troubleshooting rather than memorized commands.
interviewer_intent: Assess whether the candidate follows a systematic root-cause elimination process rather than jumping to tool-specific fixes, and whether they understand why certain replication problems become unrecoverable over time.
question: You inherit an environment where a branch-office DC has been silently failing to replicate for an unknown period. repadmin shows Event ID 2042 against it. Walk me through exactly how you'd assess and resolve this, and explain why timing matters.
good_answer: Candidate checks repadmin /showrepl for the exact failure duration, checks it against the tombstone lifetime, and recognizes that once exceeded, the DC can't be trusted to safely rejoin replication - it needs forced removal/metadata cleanup or a rebuild, not a reconnect.
excellent_answer: All of the above, plus: proactively explains they'd first confirm this isn't an intentional disconnection (e.g. a staging DC awaiting deployment) before treating it as a fault, checks whether the DC held any FSMO roles that need reassessment, and proposes a monitoring threshold well under the tombstone lifetime so this class of incident is caught long before it becomes unrecoverable next time.
weak_answer_warning: A candidate who jumps straight to 'just force a repadmin /replicate to fix it' without checking the failure duration against the tombstone lifetime is missing the core judgment this question tests - forcing replication on a tombstone-lifetime-exceeded DC does not fix the underlying problem and can reintroduce lingering objects.
follow_up_questions: What's the default tombstone lifetime, and where would you find your forest's actual configured value?
How would this scenario change if the affected DC held a FSMO role?
practical_example: A regional office DC behind a misconfigured firewall silently stopped replicating for 200+ days; repadmin only surfaced the problem when a helpdesk ticket about stale group memberships led an engineer to check replication health directly.

title: Senior AD Engineer: FSMO Seizure Judgment Call
summary: Scenario question testing judgment on transfer vs seize and the risk of a role holder returning unexpectedly.
role: Senior Active Directory Engineer / Infrastructure Lead
interviewer_intent: Test whether the candidate treats FSMO seizure as a serious, one-way decision with real failure modes, not a routine PowerShell one-liner.
question: A DC holding the RID Master role has been unreachable for six hours after a datacenter network incident. The on-call engineer wants to seize the role immediately. What questions do you ask before agreeing, and what's your actual recommendation?
good_answer: Candidate asks whether the outage is confirmed permanent or could resolve once the network incident clears, points out that RID exhaustion is rarely urgent within hours (existing DCs have their own pools), and recommends waiting for confirmation rather than seizing prematurely - while being ready to seize if the outage proves genuinely long-term.
excellent_answer: All of the above, plus explicitly flags the seize-then-original-comes-back-online risk as the specific hazard driving the caution, proposes a concrete waiting threshold tied to actual RID pool exhaustion risk rather than an arbitrary time limit, and notes that if seizure does become necessary, the original DC must be isolated or rebuilt before ever reconnecting.
weak_answer_warning: A candidate who says 'just seize it, better safe than sorry' without asking whether the outage is confirmed permanent is missing the actual risk this question is built around - premature seizure creates the dual-role-holder hazard this whole topic exists to prevent.
follow_up_questions: Would your answer change if the affected role were the Schema Master instead of RID Master?
What's your standing policy for pre-designating standby FSMO holders?
practical_example: A team seized the PDC Emulator role during what turned out to be a 45-minute network blip, then the original DC came back online mid-incident still believing it held the role, causing conflicting time-sync and password-processing behavior until manually resolved.

title: Infrastructure Architect: Justifying a Forest Recovery Investment
summary: Scenario question testing ability to communicate forest recovery readiness (or lack thereof) to non-technical stakeholders.
interviewer_intent: Assess whether the candidate can translate a technical readiness gap (untested forest recovery plan) into a business risk conversation, not just recite the recovery steps.
question: Your organization has never actually tested its Active Directory forest recovery plan, though a document exists. The CIO asks why this matters if backups exist. How do you explain the risk and what do you propose?
good_answer: Candidate explains that an untested plan routinely fails on details (wrong backup selected, DSRM passwords lost, unclear DC inventory) exactly when pressure is highest, and proposes an annual recovery drill in an isolated lab plus keeping the DC inventory/role table current.
excellent_answer: All of the above, plus quantifies the business risk in terms of realistic recovery time objective (RTO) if the plan fails on first real attempt versus a rehearsed one, ties the drill cadence to any Enterprise/Domain Admins membership changes as Microsoft recommends, and proposes the isolated-lab drill format specifically so the rehearsal itself carries zero production risk.
weak_answer_warning: A candidate who answers only 'we should test it sometime' without naming what specifically tends to fail in an untested plan (backup currency, DSRM passwords, DC role inventory) hasn't demonstrated they understand why rehearsal matters versus just having a document.
follow_up_questions: What DSRM password practices would you recommend, and why does that matter for recovery?
How would you structure the DC inventory table Microsoft's guide recommends maintaining?
practical_example: An organization discovered during a real recovery attempt that its documented DSRM passwords were years out of date because password rotation policy didn't cover them, adding hours to an already-critical outage.

title: AD Specialist: Explaining Kerberos Delegation Risk to a Security Team
summary: Scenario question testing ability to translate delegation-type risk into terms a security/audit team understands.
interviewer_intent: Test whether the candidate can explain why unconstrained delegation is a finding worth remediating, in terms a non-AD-specialist security reviewer will understand.
question: A security audit flags a service account with unconstrained Kerberos delegation and asks you to explain the risk in plain terms and propose a remediation path. What do you say?
good_answer: Candidate explains that unconstrained delegation lets that service impersonate any user to any other service in the forest if compromised, which is a much bigger blast radius than the specific service's normal job requires, and proposes migrating to constrained delegation or RBCD depending on whether cross-domain/cross-forest access is needed.
excellent_answer: All of the above, plus proposes a concrete migration plan (inventory what the service actually needs to delegate to, configure the narrower delegation type, test in a controlled window, then remove the unconstrained grant), and notes RBCD's advantage of putting control in the resource owner's hands rather than requiring domain-admin-level changes for every new consumer.
weak_answer_warning: A candidate who can't explain why unconstrained delegation is worse than constrained delegation in concrete impersonation terms - only that 'Microsoft doesn't recommend it' - hasn't demonstrated real understanding of the mechanism being flagged.
follow_up_questions: When would RBCD be the only viable option compared to constrained delegation?
How would you find every account in the forest currently holding unconstrained delegation?
practical_example: A legacy application server was found holding unconstrained delegation rights years after its original justification (a since-decommissioned integration) had disappeared, representing exactly the kind of forgotten, unreviewed grant audits are designed to catch.

title: PowerShell Automation Engineer: Designing gMSA Rollout for a Growing Farm
summary: Scenario question testing whether the candidate designs for scale (group-based authorization) rather than one-off host entries.
interviewer_intent: Check whether the candidate designs gMSA authorization for operational scale rather than manual per-host edits.
question: You're rolling out a gMSA for a web farm that will grow from 3 to 30 servers over the next year, with servers added via an automated pipeline. How do you design the authorization so new servers don't require a manual gMSA edit each time?
good_answer: Candidate creates a dedicated AD security group, sets PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword to that group rather than individual host accounts, and has the provisioning pipeline add each new server's computer account to the group automatically.
excellent_answer: All of the above, plus flags the group-membership replication delay as something the pipeline needs to account for (a brand-new host may need to wait for replication before Install-ADServiceAccount succeeds), and recommends Test-ADServiceAccount as an automated post-provisioning health check rather than a manual step.
weak_answer_warning: A candidate who proposes adding each new server's computer account directly to PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword one at a time hasn't designed for the stated scale requirement and will require a gMSA object edit for every one of the 27 future servers.
follow_up_questions: What would you monitor to catch a new host that fails to retrieve the gMSA password after provisioning?
How does this design change if the farm spans multiple domains?
practical_example: A team that authorized gMSA access per-host manually fell behind their autoscaling pipeline, causing new instances to fail service startup until someone noticed and manually added each one - exactly the operational drag a group-based design avoids.
